research.description: Sepia studio bust portrait in an oval vignette on a card mount: a man in his late twenties or thirties with a full trimmed beard, wearing a sack coat and a wide, soft bow tie — costume and mount conventions of the 1870s-1880s carte-de-visite/cabinet-card era. The BLD filename identifies him as Reznor Stewart, the Beaumont pioneer who took up a homestead south of the railroad in 1883 and built the Stewart Ranch to more than 2,200 acres (BLD/Calisphere), later co-founding the Beaumont Bank (built 1911) and serving as its president for several years; the family name survives in Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery. His daughter Laura May was born c. 1884 and his son Reznor P. Stewart Jr. in 1890 (Find A Grave), so a portrait of him as a young man belongs to the 1870s-1880s — the catalog's former 1900-1915 range is too late for both the sitter's apparent age and the card format. The sitter cannot be Reznor Jr., who died at 16 in 1907.
corrections: Date corrected 1900-1915 → c. 1870s-1880s: the old range was a folder-level guess; costume, card format, and biographical anchors (homestead 1883; children born 1884/1890) all point two to four decades earlier.

research.description: A studio cabinet-card portrait of Captain John Morongo in a three-piece suit and bow tie, made at Cramer's California Gallery, 402 Kearny Street, San Francisco. Hereditary leader of the Serrano Maarrenga'yam clan and the first officially recognized 'captain' of the Potrero (San Gorgonio) reservation, Morongo served for years on the U.S. Indian police, spoke fluent English, campaigned for public schooling and against liquor sales, and was the leader whose family name the reservation and Band formally adopted. The exact print survives at the Huntington Library among the papers of W. H. Weinland, the Moravian missionary at Morongo, inscribed 'The late Capt. John Morongo... A noble Indian.'
corrections: The old label 'Morongo Band of Mission Indians, 1908' misdescribed a named individual as an anonymous group.
The 1908 date is impossible for a life portrait: two 1898 newspapers report Morongo's death at the Banning reservation in July 1898. '1908' is the year the reservation formally took the Morongo name.
Likely source of the date confusion: his brother Francisco died in 1906.

research.original_title: Beaumont Vista With Hotel Beaumont Visible To Right Of Town Undated
research.description: Distant view of the young town of Beaumont from the brush-covered hills south of town, looking north across the open San Gorgonio Pass plain to the San Bernardino Mountains, with a dirt wagon road dropping through the chaparral in the foreground. The settlement is a thin scatter of frame buildings on a treeless plain, and the large multi-story block at its right (east) edge is identified by the collection as the Hotel Beaumont — the 'beautiful and costly' hotel the Southern California Investment Co. built in 1887 as the town's third hotel to attract land buyers, which 'stood unused for years' after the 1888 boom collapse and was destroyed by a kitchen fire in 1909. The standing hotel brackets the view between 1887 and 1909, and the town's sparseness suggests the earlier half of that range. A handwritten negative number reading '2099' shows at lower left — the mark of a commercial view photographer's numbered series (the C.C. Pierce / California Historical Society series at USC uses corner numbers of this kind), not yet identified. The 960 × 733 px digital file is consistent with a web download from an online library rather than an in-house scan.

research.original_title: Hotel Beaumont And Beaumont Train Station And Peter Allen Store Postcard Front Fr Karen Sumner Noordman
research.description: Elevated postcard view (front of the card) over Beaumont's depot quarter: the long single-story Southern Pacific depot — the 'larger train depot' the railroad built in 1887, the same year it officially renamed the station from San Gorgonio to Beaumont — fills the right foreground beside a small trackside shed and multiple track lines. Across the open dirt forecourt, where a horse team stands, is Peter Allen's false-fronted general store, its parapet signed 'STORE' and its porch fascia 'PETER ALLEN' over goods and figures under the awning; a second scallop-parapeted false-front store stands to its right (sign not legible at this resolution), with a windmill and the scattered cottages of the young town on the treeless plain behind. On the knoll at far right rises the three-story, tower-and-cupola-topped Hotel Beaumont, built 1887 by the Southern California Investment Co. and destroyed by a kitchen fire in 1909, which brackets the scene between 1887 and August 1909. The scan came from the Karen Sumner Noordman collection in January 2023; only the card front is present in the archive.

research.description: A rare interior view of a real estate banquet at the Edinburgh Hotel, preserved as a rounded-corner print on a black album page bearing the typed label "EDINBURGH HOTEL / REAL ESTATE BANQUET." Families in Edwardian dress — including several children and a baby in a bonnet — sit at round, white-clothed tables beneath interior columns and an early chandelier, most faces turned toward the camera, with a second set table visible at right. Per the Calisphere description, John D. Revis is turned toward J. Drew Funk, the young man at the center of the photo. The three-story Victorian building opened in 1887 as the Beaumont Hotel, later closed, reopened in 1907 as the Hotel Edinburgh, and came to a fiery end in August 1909; it stood on Beaumont Avenue where the El Rancho Restaurant and Best Western Rancho Motel were later located.

research.description: Vignetted studio bust portrait of Reznor Perry Stewart in a striped sack suit and patterned four-in-hand tie, with a full greying beard and swept-back hair. Stewart homesteaded at Beaumont in 1883 and, adding purchased Southern Pacific railroad land, built a grain and hay ranch of about 2,200 acres — one of the pass's major operations; Holmes' 1912 county history records that 'R. P. Stewart and Dan Scott commenced raising grain' in 1884, the year settlement began in earnest. He went on to be a founder and long-time president of the Beaumont Bank (built 1911 in the Funk Building, 248 W. 5th St.), and the family name survives in Stewart Park (named in his honor, per SGPHS) and on the 'Stewart Sunny Slope Cemetery' entrance arch; his daughter Laura May Stewart appears with him in SGPHS ranch photographs, and Stewart-family material at the Beaumont Library District carries Laura May Stewart Trust rights. The vignetted cabinet-style format and his costume suggest the 1890s-1900s; his birth and death dates were not located in the sources searched this session.

research.original_title: Beaumont Land And Water Pumping Station From Beaumont Library District
research.description: A gable-roofed frame pump house stands in a brushy canyon bottom near Beaumont, with a tall well-drilling derrick rising immediately behind it; several workmen and a saddled horse are spaced along the dirt road in the foreground. The print carries the 'BEAUMONT LAND AND WATER COMPANY' stamp across its top edge and the handwritten caption 'Pumping Plant No. 1' along the bottom. Calisphere's context note traces what followed: after the Beaumont Irrigation District purchased the Beaumont Land and Water Company, the District drilled roughly 35 exploratory holes in the Edgar Canyon area through the 1920s and into the 1930s, developing small producing wells upstream of groundwater faults. This photograph records the company's original No. 1 pumping plant from the earlier, pre-District era.

research.description: Vertical photograph of a large crowd — men in suits and brimmed hats, women in white blouses and long skirts, boys in overalls — gathered on a brushy slope around a flowing well, with water pouring from a pipe into a wooden flume and a standpipe rising at right. research.description: A team of roughly two dozen horses and mules, strung out to the right, pulls a combined harvester through standing grain in a dusty field, its long header and draper frame extending to the left; at least three crew members ride the machine, and the bare foothills of the San Gorgonio Pass close the horizon. The scene belongs to the Stewart Ranch, the grain and hay operation Reznor Perry Stewart built from his 1883 Beaumont homestead — Holmes (1912) records R. P. Stewart raising grain from 1884 and still on the ranch in 1912, and the print sits in the BLD Reznor Stewart folder. Two visually distinct Calisphere prints show the same operation's harvest crews, one of them dated 1900 with Jim Barrett named as driver. Big-team combine harvesting of this kind was practiced in inland Southern California from the 1890s into the 1920s, so the existing c. 1900–1930 range is retained; the print itself is undated.

research.original_title: Egan Ave Block From Beaumont Library District
research.description: A printed commercial postcard captioned 'EAGAN AVENUE, BEAUMONT, CAL.' looking along the unpaved avenue: the two-story Summit House hotel, its porch sign legible, stands at left behind a row of trees; an early automobile is mid-street and the false-front commercial row lines the right side. The Summit House was Beaumont's first hotel — Frank Mindler converted the Beatty Boarding House into it in 1884 to lodge prospective land buyers (BLD local history; Calisphere/Banning metadata), and it burned down in 1925. The automobile and the letterpress-caption postcard format place the view roughly 1905-1920, comfortably before the fire. 'Eagan' is the printer's variant spelling of Egan Avenue, named for town founder George C. Egan. The collection filename records the scan as received from the Beaumont Library District and places the view in the 600 block of Egan (unverified).

research.original_title: Egan Ave Postcard Courtesy Steve Lech Postcard Collection
research.description: A hand-tinted printed postcard titled on its face 'Egan Avenue, looking South, Beaumont, Cal.' with the imprint 'Robert Fulton, Publisher.' It shows the dirt avenue lined with a two-story wooden false-front store whose sign reads '[A. —] GENERAL MERCHANDISE' (first line only partly legible; plausibly A.T. Ganty's store, which by 1915 occupied a stone block on this street), smaller awninged storefronts, and horse-drawn wagons — no automobiles. A 1915-postmarked postcard of the same street in this collection already shows the stone 'A.T. Ganty General Merchandise' block and parked autos, so this all-wood, all-horse view is earlier, c. 1905–1910, on a card format (front title band) typical of c. 1907–1915 printings. The scan comes courtesy of the Steve Lech postcard collection.

research.description: A mounted photographic print looking along unpaved Beaumont Avenue: a double row of tall eucalyptus at left, fenced fields, utility poles, a horse-drawn buggy in the roadway, and a farmhouse among younger trees at right. The print carries a typed label 'BEAUMONT AVE', a purple rubber stamp reading 'BEAUMONT LAND AND WATER COMPANY', and 'Beaumont Ave' in ink along the bottom margin. The Beaumont Land and Water Company was incorporated at Riverside in mid-August 1907 (Riverside Enterprise and San Bernardino Sun, Aug. 17, 1907) under president Clarendon B. Eyer, and per the Los Angeles Herald of Aug. 18, 1909 it purchased the Beaumont hotel, townsite, lands and water in August 1907 from the San Francisco bank that had held them since the 1890s foreclosure, then promoted the town aggressively from Los Angeles offices. The company stamp therefore places this print in that promotional era, and the timeline's 'c. 1900' date was an unsourced AI estimate. A caveat: an earlier 'Beaumont Land and Water company' appears in an 1894 Riverside Enterprise item, so a 1890s stamp cannot be absolutely excluded, but the typed office label and the 1907–08 promotion campaign make the later era far more likely.
corrections: Date changed from flat 'c. 1900' (AI-authored SGPHS-timeline estimate) to c. 1905–1912, anchored on the print's Beaumont Land and Water Company stamp and the company's documented August 1907 incorporation and townsite purchase.

research.description: A screened halftone portrait, reproduced from an unidentified printed publication, of Reznor Perry Stewart (3 Nov 1845 - 12 Nov 1933), seated in three-quarter view with a full white beard, dark suit, and watch chain. Stewart was one of Beaumont's founding ranchers: Holmes' 1912 county history records that 'R. P. Stewart and Dan Scott commenced raising grain' in 1884 and that Stewart was still living on his grain and hay ranch in 1912, and BLD's Calisphere Beaumont Bank item adds that he was one of the founders of the Beaumont Bank (built 1911) and its president for several years. The family name survives in Stewart Ranch and in Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery, Beaumont, where he is buried with his daughter Laura May (1884-1974) and son Reznor P. Jr. (1890-1907). His apparent age — sixties to seventies — against the 1845 birth date places the sitting around 1905-1920. This is print 'c' of three copies of the same portrait in the BLD folder; the publication it came from has not been identified, and the Google-scanned volume of the 1912 county history contains no Stewart portrait or biography.

research.original_title: Beaumont Train Depot After Expansion Remodel
research.description: Black-and-white printed postcard captioned 'Station, Beaumont, Cal.': a steam locomotive pulls in past the two-story, half-timbered Southern Pacific depot while men wait on the platform, a woman in a white shirtwaist stands by the door, and a baggage cart sits at right. A depot and telegraph office were established here in 1875, when the site — then called Summit — marked the highest point on the SP line through San Gorgonio Pass; the original station was 'a small red building,' and the railroad 'built a large depot about 1887' (Holmes 1912), the structure shown here. No source was found for the working title's claim that this view follows an 'expansion remodel' around 1909; the building is best identified as the c. 1887 depot as it stood in the postcard era, c. 1905-1915. It was aging by then: in January 1914 SP assistant superintendent Sloan remarked that 'the S.P. needed a new depot in Beaumont,' preferring a site at the Apex. The 1939 press still located Beaumont's Egan Avenue business center 'north of the Southern Pacific depot.'
corrections: Dropped the unsupported 'after expansion remodel' framing: no newspaper or county-history source documents a c. 1909 depot remodel; the two-story building matches the 'large depot' SP built about 1887, which replaced the original small red station of 1875.

research.original_title: Beaumont Land And Water Company From Beaumont Library District
research.description: A mounted print, hand-captioned 'Office at Beaumont' on the mat, showing the Beaumont Land and Water Company's small Mission Revival office: tiled parapet roof with scrolled end caps, three arched bays, a fresh concrete sidewalk, and an unpaved street. The main signboard reads 'Beaumont Land and Water Co.'; the left window carries arched lettering reading '[S]an Gorgonio / Water Co.' and the right window 'Land … Water Co.' The company purchased the Beaumont townsite and several thousand adjoining acres and promoted them relentlessly — 453 Chronicling America hits, overwhelmingly the Los Angeles Herald, run from Oct. 6, 1907 through 1910, recording biweekly excursions, day-and-night well drilling (1908), the Cherry Valley subdivision (1908), the La Mesa Miravilla tract (1909), and enlarged Los Angeles headquarters at 616 South Broadway (1909). That campaign drove the boom that carried Beaumont to incorporation on Nov. 18, 1912. The building's style and new-built appearance place the photograph within the company's active years, c. 1907-1915 — the company is not documented before 1907, so the previous 1890-1905 range cannot stand.
corrections: Date corrected from c. 1890-1905 to c. 1907-1915: the company is not documented before October 1907, and a tiled-parapet Mission Revival office is anachronistic for the 1890s.
Window lettering ('[S]an Gorgonio / Water Co.' left, 'Land … Water Co.' right) read from enlarged crops of the print and added to the record.
Historical context added: the company's townsite purchase and 1907-1910 sales campaign (LA Herald via Chronicling America) preceding Beaumont's 1912 incorporation.

research.original_title: Hotel Beaumont Renamed Hotel Edinburgh Postcard
research.description: Hand-colored postcard captioned 'Hotel Edinburgh, Beaumont, California,' showing the twin-towered Queen Anne boom hotel behind mature gardens and palms. Built in 1887 at a cost of $40,000 as the Beaumont Hotel — Beaumont's third hotel, erected by the investment company that bought Egan's property to lure land buyers during the boom — it stood largely idle after the 1888 bust, was renovated and reopened in 1907 under the new name Edinburgh Hotel, and was destroyed by fire on August 16, 1909 (BLD/Calisphere). It stood at Fifth Street and Beaumont Avenue, roughly where I-10 now crosses Beaumont Avenue. Because the card bears the Edinburgh name, the view and publication belong to the c. 1907-1909 window. The file is a small web scan bearing an ePodunk.com watermark at lower right, not a library original.
corrections: Date narrowed 1900-1909 → c. 1907-1909: the 'Edinburgh' name was only in use from the 1907 reopening to the August 16, 1909 fire.

research.original_title: First Bank Of Beaumont Construction From Calisphere
research.description: Album-mounted photograph labeled in type 'Old Bank Building, Fifth and California' and stamped 'Photo by Salvage,' showing the Bank of Beaumont building topped out but not yet roofed — rusticated cement-block first story, brick second story — with the construction crew posed among brick piles and lumber on the dirt street. The bank organized in 1908 with $25,000 capital and deliberately deferred opening until it had its own building: on August 27, 1908 the directors approved a two-story fire-proof cement-and-brick block at Fifth Street and California Avenue and called for bids; contractor George Mayer won the work, subletting the masonry to T. O. M. Jones; and the bank opened its doors in the finished ~$8,000 building on Monday, April 12, 1909. C. B. Eyer and R. P. Stewart sat on the first board with Kenneth R. Smoot among the stockholders — a 1939 retrospective compressed this to 'Eyer and Smoot built the first Bank of Beaumont building' — and by 1939 the building served as irrigation district headquarters. The photographer, Salvage, advertised in Beaumont's Gateway Gazette in December 1908 and left town in June 1909, which together with the construction stage brackets this view to the fall and winter of 1908-09.
corrections: Date grounded and widened from '1909' to 1908-1909: directors approved the building and called bids August 27, 1908; the bank opened in the finished building Monday, April 12, 1909 — so this roofless view is fall/winter 1908-09.

Photographer identified: the purple 'Photo by Salvage' stamp matches Salvage, the photographer advertising in Beaumont's Gateway Gazette December 1908 - June 1909 ('your picture taken and finished on a postal card. SALVAGE, Photographer').

Builder credited correctly: contractor George Mayer with masonry by T. O. M. Jones (1909 opening article); the 1939 'Eyer and Smoot built it' line is retrospective shorthand for the boom's leading capitalists, who were among the bank's directors/stockholders.
Building's afterlife added: 'the building now used as irrigation district headquarters' (1939).

research.original_title: Eucalyptus Trees In Beaumont Vintage Postcard Looking North On Beaumont Ave
research.description: Hand-colored printed postcard captioned on its face 'Beaumont Ave., Beaumont, Cal.,' showing the unpaved avenue running between rows of tall mature street trees, with a Craftsman-style house at right and hills in the distance. The working filename identifies the trees as eucalyptus and the view as looking north; neither can be confirmed from the front of the card alone, but Beaumont's signature street trees — eucalyptus and pepper — were planted along roughly twenty miles of newly laid-out streets by the Southern California Investment Company during the 1887 boom, and Holmes' 1912 county history notes the trees had made excellent growth even while most streets sat unused through the town's long post-1888 slump. The Craftsman-style house and the card's hand-tinted, pre-WWI format fit the assigned c. 1908-1915 window — the years when the Beaumont Land and Water Company's 1907 revival under C. B. Eyer brought new houses to the tree-lined avenues.

research.original_title: Gateway Gazette Interior Postcard Leslie Rios
research.description: Blue-monochrome halftone postcard captioned "A corner in the Gateway Gazette composing room, Beaumont, Cal.", showing the interior of the weekly paper's plant: banks of type cases along the left wall, sloped composing benches with more cases at right, work tables, and a man — evidently a compositor — standing at left holding a sheet of paper. The Gateway Gazette launched in late January 1908 under editor Arthur J. Burdick in a purpose-built office (LA Herald, Jan 19, 1908) and was still publishing under Burdick in July 1909. A later hand, in blue ink across the right margin, adds a first-person provenance note: "I worked in this place setting type in 1911. My name was Edvige Hamel, now Mrs. Edvige Smith" — direct testimony that the paper's composing room was operating with hand-set type in 1911. The annotation's phrasing ("my name was... now Mrs. ...") and modern ink show it was written years after the card was printed. Companion to the exterior office view img_f711da54b73a8423 in the same collection.

research.original_title: Gateway Gazette Beaumont Leslie Rios Postcards
research.description: Blue-monochrome halftone postcard captioned "The office of the Gateway Gazette as it now appears, Beaumont, Cal.", showing the paper's small false-front frame office with plate-glass show windows, a recessed entry, and a partly obscured roofline sign reading "[Gatew]ay Gazette". The Gateway Gazette was Beaumont's weekly newspaper, launched during the town's 1907-09 land boom: the Los Angeles Herald of January 19, 1908 reported that "the building for the new printing establishment is about completed and next Thursday the first issue of the Gateway Gazette, a Beaumont paper, will be added to the state's newspaper list, under the editorship of Arthur J. Burdick, formerly one of the editors of the Los Angeles Evening News." A full-page Beaumont Land and Water Company promotion in the Herald of April 13, 1908 quotes "the Gateway Gazette, Beaumont's weekly newspaper" on the town's bank organization, gas-and-electric company, and new volunteer fire department, and Burdick was still bylined "Editor Beaumont Gateway Gazette" in the Herald of July 18, 1909. The "as it now appears" phrasing and the boom-era promotional style date the card to the paper's early years, when the purpose-built office (completed January 1908) was new. A companion card in the same collection shows the composing room interior (img_19665af80792888c).

research.description: A very small (170×214 px) thumbnail of the front page of The Gateway Gazette of Beaumont for Thursday, April 30, 1908. The visible headlines — 'Products of Beaumont Soil' at upper left and 'Will Hold An Apple Fai[r]' at right — match the digitized issue held by the California Digital Newspaper Collection, which catalogs the paper under 'Daily Gazette (Beaumont)': Volume I, Number 15, 30 April 1908, downloadable as an 18 MB four-page PDF. The Gateway Gazette was Beaumont's boom-era weekly: the Riverside Enterprise of Jan. 22, 1908 announced 'the first number of the Gateway Gazette, a new weekly paper, will be issued at Beaumont' the next day, naming Arthur J. Burdick of the Gateway Gazette in its Personals, and the Los Angeles Herald of Jan. 26, 1908 confirmed the new paper 'made its appearance last Thursday' (Jan. 23, 1908). Number 15 on April 30 is exactly 14 weeks after that first issue, corroborating the date. The issue also reports an S.P. general manager's special-train visit and the Beaumont women's Orange Festival.

research.description: A black album-page scan holds a rounded-corner print of a dirt wagon track curving through oak-shaded Edgar Canyon, north of Beaumont. A handful of men stand in the grass at center around a light wooden well-drilling derrick, with another figure walking the track at left. The typed mount label reads 'WATER WELL DRILLING / EDGAR CANYON / 1908.' The exploration located faults and groundwater barriers that pooled water underground, allowing the District to develop small producing wells upstream of them.

research.description: Page 6 of the Los Angeles Herald of Wednesday, August 18, 1909, dominated by 'Spectacular Fire at Beaumont Destroys Hotel Edinburgh, Landmark of Community' with a halftone of the hotel; the page layout in the catalog image (including 'Would Educate All Foreigners', 'Very Human Is Royal Family' and the Globe Savings Bank advertisement) matches the CDNC scan. The article (dateline Beaumont, Aug. 17) reports the three-story, 70-room frame hotel — 'the next largest hotel building in Riverside county' — totally destroyed about 11 o'clock the previous night, i.e. the night of August 16–17, 1909, a $45,000–$50,000 loss against $10,000 insurance; operator David Cochrane (formerly of Riverside's Hotel Hollyrood) was away, though his wife was in the building, and the four-acre park's trees were scorched. The Herald recounts that F. P. Sigler, 'original founder of the town of Beaumont,' spent $44,000 on the hotel (the Herald says built 1890; a Feb. 1908 Gazette retrospective shows the same house advertised as the 'Beaumont' hotel in a Sentinel of about 1888 and 'now known as Hotel Edinburgh'), lost it in the 1893 panic to a San Francisco bank, after which it stood closed until the Beaumont Land and Water Company bought hotel, townsite, lands and water in August 1907 and refurnished it. The record therefore depicts a newspaper page, not an original photograph: its date is the publication date, and the hotel's name at destruction was Hotel Edinburgh — 'Beaumont Hotel' was the building's original 1880s name.
corrections: Title/caption corrected from 'Beaumont Hotel fire' to Hotel Edinburgh — the hotel's name at its destruction; the 1908 Gazette retrospective confirms it began as the 'Beaumont' hotel and was renamed, so the timeline's renaming claim was right but the display name was anachronistic.
Fire dated precisely: night of August 16–17, 1909; the record's own date is the Aug. 18 publication date.

Depot, Beaumont' on the negative, showing a ground-level view along the Southern Pacific depot platform: roughly two dozen people — men in hats with baggage, children, and two women in ankle-length Edwardian dress at right — under pepper trees, with tracks curving through the foreground and a two-way directional arrow sign mounted on a platform post. The frame depot with hipped roof was built about 1887, when the railroad enlarged its Beaumont facilities (Holmes 1912; BLD's Calisphere depot item CBEA_134 gives the same date). The 1909 date is carried from the collection filename — most plausibly a postmark on the unscanned verso — and is consistent with the clothing and the real-photo-postcard era. Calisphere holds a different exposure of the same depot (an elevated view looking east with a train alongside and the 'BEAUMONT' station sign); this street-level postcard view does not appear in the BLD Calisphere collection.
corrections: Completed the truncated caption ('Beaumont train depot 1909 postcard from') and retitled from the caption inscribed on the postcard itself: 'S. P. Depot, Beaumont'.
Added depot construction date c. 1887 (Holmes 1912: 'having built a large depot about 1887'; same date in Calisphere CBEA_134).
Flagged the 1909 date as filename-derived (verso/postmark not in the scan) — retained but marked unverified.
Rights determined as Public domain (rule 2: commercially published pre-1931 postcard).
Adversarial review 2026-07-22: downgraded rights from Public domain to Unclear - PD claim rested on inferred (not demonstrated) pre-1931 publication.

research.description: Tinted real-photo postcard of the Southern Pacific depot at Beaumont, California, with thirteen men and boys — at least five holding bicycles — posed on the platform, a steaming train at right, and San Gorgonio Pass foothills in the distance. The station board reads 'To San Francisco 562 7/10 M. / B[ea]umont / [Elev]ation 2556 Feet / To New Orleans 1925 4/10 M.' (the SP Sunset Route mileage format), and 'S.P. Depot Beaumont' is written along the bottom. The card was mailed to Miss Lula Wheeler of Melrose, Texas ('How are you I am fine Come where oranges grow, Hudson Hall') and is dated by its March 28, 1909 postmark; the arc cancel visible on the catalog copy reads '…GDOCHES' — Nacogdoches, the town nearest Melrose — matching that transit. Because it is a 'Beaumont' card it entered the Tyrrell Historical Library in Beaumont, TEXAS (Southeast Texas Postcards Collection), whose own catalog record confirms the subject is Beaumont, California, noting the two Beaumonts 'are sometimes mistaken for one another'; the mountainous backdrop is impossible for coastal-plain Beaumont, Texas. The catalog's copy is a 729×461 screenshot watermarked 'TYRRELL HISTORICAL LIBRARY'; The Portal to Texas History serves an unwatermarked 1500×980 scan of the front (and 1500×990 of the back). The previous credit 'Tyrrell Historical Library / Calisphere' was wrong about Calisphere — the digitization is a Portal to Texas History item.
corrections: Confirmed the depot is Beaumont, CALIFORNIA — elevation-2,556-ft SP station board with San Francisco/New Orleans mileages, mountain backdrop, and the Tyrrell catalog's own statement — despite the holding library being in Beaumont, Texas.
Removed the erroneous 'Calisphere' half of the old credit: the digitization is by The Portal to Texas History (UNT), not Calisphere.
Date refined from a bare '1909' to the documented March 28, 1909 postmark; explained the Nacogdoches (Texas) cancel as the Melrose, Texas delivery route, not evidence of a Texas subject.
Flagged the catalog image as a watermarked low-res screenshot and supplied the 1500×980 unwatermarked master.

Decoupled this record from the SGPHS timeline's March 1909 S.P. demonstration-train story — the demo train is a separate photograph (SP No. 2789, per earlier re-identification); this card simply shows the depot.

research.original_title: Beaumont Post Office Ne Corner Fifth St And Egan Ave
research.description: Real-photo postcard, captioned 'Post Office Beaumont Calif.' in white script in the negative, photographed here as an album-page print with black mounting corners. It shows the small false-front frame post office ('Post Office, Beaumont, Cal.' painted on the false front and porch beam), a group of men and women in c. 1910 dress beneath a large eucalyptus, a horse-drawn wagon at right, and a dirt street. At left stands a tile-roofed pavilion with fluted columns on rusticated-block pedestals — a visual match to the W.C.T.U. drinking-fountain shelter seen in the catalog's fountain-dedication prints — so the view postdates the fountain's dedication (1910 per the catalog's dedication prints; 'Spring 1911' per BLD/Calisphere). The corner is disputed: the filename says northeast corner of 5th and Egan, but BLD's Calisphere description of the 1890s view of this intersection places the old post office on the southwest corner.

research.original_title: Beaumont Post Office And Dedication Of The Wtcu Fountain B
research.description: A real-photo postcard captioned in the negative 'W.C.T.U. Fountain, Beaumont Calif': a crowd in Edwardian dress — women in wide hats, a man in a long coat and derby at left — gathers at a hip-roofed pavilion whose classical columns are wound with garlands for the ceremony. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union fountain was presented to Beaumont at 5th Street and Egan Avenue; BLD's Calisphere metadata for a related dedication postcard (CBEA_040) dates the event 'about 1910-1911' (Spring 1911) and notes the fountain survives, relocated to 7th, Egan and California Streets. The collection filename says 1910, so the date is carried as 1910-1911. The clapboard building behind the pavilion is identified by the filename as the Beaumont post office, which nothing in the image confirms. The scan bears an 'LKCA' watermark, indicating it was taken from a dealer or auction listing; the same scan is filed twice in the collection (the 'a' copy is catalog record img_7547c2a1a3855993).
corrections: 'WTCU' corrected to 'W.C.T.U.' (Woman's Christian Temperance Union) — the filename transposed the letters.
Date widened from 1910 to 1910-1911: BLD's Calisphere metadata dates the dedication Spring 1911.

The post-office identification is demoted to unverified — nothing in the image confirms the building behind the pavilion, and the related Calisphere dedication view places the crowd in front of a general-merchandise store at 5th and Egan.
Noted the duplicate scan filed as img_7547c2a1a3855993 ('a' copy, Beaumont Post Office folder) — candidates for cross-linking.
Rights upgraded from Unclear to Public domain: a real-photo postcard produced for sale c. 1910-1911, published before 1931 (rule 2).

research.description: An elderly man with a full white beard, wearing a broad-brimmed hat and a vest over a work shirt, stands behind a wire fence in front of a ranch house, with garden flowers at lower right — a small amateur snapshot, unannotated and low-resolution in this copy. Stewart, 88 years old and prominent in affairs...', and Notices to Creditors for his estate (No. 6530, with Laura M. Stewart as special administrator) ran in the Beaumont Daily Gazette from January 1934. His evident old age places the snapshot in roughly his last two decades, not the catalog's former 1900-1915 range. In 1962 Beaumont's cemetery was renamed Stewart Sunny Slope Cemetery in his family's honor.

research.description: Real-photo postcard, hand-titled on the negative "W.C.T.U. Fountain Beaumont Calif", showing roughly two dozen women in dark Edwardian dress and wide-brimmed hats — with a few children and a dog — gathered at a four-columned, tile-roofed pavilion sheltering a fieldstone drinking fountain, a clapboard building behind. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union presented the fountain to Beaumont at Fifth Street and Egan Avenue and dedicated it on Christmas Day, December 25, 1910 — a date confirmed independently by a 1959 Record Gazette retrospective, a 2011 Press-Enterprise centennial piece, and the City of Beaumont's own account of the plaque reading "WCTU Dec. 25, 1910". The Rios-collection provenance identifies this as the dedication gathering itself. research.original_title: First Library House In Basement Of Bank Building
research.description: The brand-new Beaumont Bank building — brick above a stuccoed ground floor, striped awnings at every window, two men idling by the chamfered corner entrance, and a 'FUNK REALTY CO. REAL ESTATE' sign on the frontage beyond. Reznor Stewart (of the Stewart Ranch) was a founder and long-time president of the bank, built in 1911 as the Funk Building at 248 West 5th Street. When Beaumont voted itself a library district on August 12, 1911 — the only library-district library in the State Library's 1912 census of California — the new library opened that October in two rented rooms on this building's ground floor, at $10 a month, and stayed until the Carnegie building opened in June 1914.

research.original_title: Laura May Stewart In Chaps Dated
research.description: Full-length outdoor portrait of a smiling young woman in a broad-brimmed hat, neckerchief, and work shirt, a rope in her right hand and a coiled lariat in her left, standing in a dirt corral yard before a plank fence, with a windmill, tank, and shed behind; the mount is inked 'Laura in chaps 1911.' She is Laura May Stewart, daughter of Stewart Ranch founder Reznor P. Stewart, aged about 26 here. Three years later she was crowned the first queen of the Beaumont Cherry Festival, riding in the 1914 parade in a Studebaker Six. She died in Beaumont in late February 1974, aged 89 (residence 1306 Palm Ave.), and her name survives in the Banning-based Laura May Stewart Trust Fund, which Calisphere records name as rights holder for the family's photographs. The snapshot is one of three 1911-dated portraits of her (in chaps, on horseback, and formal) in the collection's Laura May Stewart folder.

research.description: A modern snapshot of a framed real-photo postcard (dark wood frame and window reflection visible): a masonry church under construction — coursed brick/block walls, tall arched windows with scaffolding visible through the openings, roof framing incomplete, a corner tower at left — amid trees bowed under heavy snow, with a mid-1910s touring car at the curb. The handwritten inscription reads 'Beaumont Calif. / The new Presbyterian Church unfinished(?) after snow storm Jan. 1[?]', with a later blue-ink year annotation most plausibly reading '1916'. The building is Beaumont's Presbyterian church at Seventh Street and Egan Avenue (701 Egan Ave) — not the congregation's later river-rock sanctuary at 7th & Euclid, which was built of Whitewater stone and completed 20 May 1934. When the rock church was finished, the Presbyterians sold the Egan Avenue building to the First Christian Church (1934), which still occupies it. The prior catalog date of c. 1930-1940 is therefore wrong: the church was 'new' and unfinished roughly two decades earlier, consistent with the automobile and the annotation.

research.description: Oval vignette portrait of Jane Eyer Smoot (1859-1935), pixel-identical to the 285x291 px image on her Find a Grave memorial captioned "Passport photo," associated there with her U.S. passport application of October 20, 1915, which lists her as age 55 and residing in Beaumont, California — the family's earliest directly documented Beaumont residence. Jane, an 1881 University of Michigan graduate and 1890s suffrage advocate who in 1894 led Highland Park, Illinois' first woman's club, was in Southern California by December 1908, when the Los Angeles Herald reported her mother Nancy A. Eyer's death at the Smoot home at 603 Esplanade, Redondo Beach; by April 1909 her husband Kenneth was vice president and her brother Clarendon B. Eyer president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company, the firm behind Beaumont's land boom. The ultimate source of this image is the passport application record preserved in NARA RG 59 (digitized in Ancestry's "U.S. Passport Applications, 1795-1925"); the catalog copy matches the Find a Grave scan contributed by D.J. McLaughlin in 2019. Jane died in Beaumont on November 25, 1935, three years after Kenneth, and is buried beside him at Hillside Memorial Park, Redlands.

research.description: A decorated Studebaker Six touring car photographed beneath a pepper tree, canopied with draped fabric and ribbons for the 2nd Cherry Festival parade; a placard at the running board is lettered "BEAUMONT GARAGE AND MACHINE CO. / STUDEBAKER SIX." and a "Studebaker" script pennant hangs at the rear, with a ribbon streaming forward to a bow at the radiator. Queen Laura Mae Stewart — the festival's first queen — is seated in the center rear seat, with Princesses Lois Behu on her right and Clara Dietrich on her left; Lawrence Rulier, in uniform up front, is the queen's escort, and E. O. Jones is the driver. Per Calisphere, the first Cherry Festival began in 1913 with great success, and the following year Laura Mae Stewart became its first queen; the Studebaker was brought out from Los Angeles to carry the queen in the parade. A second open car and a house are visible in the background.
corrections: Date corrected from 1919 to 1914: Calisphere identifies this as the 2nd Cherry Festival (the first festival was 1913, and Laura Mae Stewart became the first queen the following year). The old 1919 date from the SGPHS timeline caption is wrong.

research.description: Real photo postcard (rubber-stamped "5th street / BEAUMONT" in red, captioned "Beaumont. Cal." in the negative) showing touring cars of the mid-1910s to early 1920s parked along a business corner, with children on the sidewalk at right. The porch sign at right reads "A. T. GANTT AND BRO. / GROCERIES - DRY GOODS": A. T. Gantt & Bro. general merchandise advertised in the Beaumont Gazette from January 1908, and the Gantt mercantile at Fifth Street and Egan Avenue was established after the family's 1906 arrival, continuing under Mrs. Brice Gantt after her husband's death c. 1927 (her 1936 obituary). Across the street, a rusticated cement-block business row carries two REAL ESTATE signs and a round sweet-shop/cigar sign — cement-block commercial construction that Beaumont adopted in 1907-08. This is the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere item CBEA_036, whose description names "Gantt, a groceries and dry goods store, a Sweet Shop offering lunches and a real estate store front" and places the view (with BLD's own question mark) on the 200 block of West 5th Street between Grace and Egan — the district around Fifth & Egan near the depot that was early Beaumont's main business section.
corrections: Matched the record to its actual Calisphere Beaumont Library District item (CBEA_036) — the earlier screening that reported no Calisphere match missed it; the BLD description independently confirms the storefront identifications.

Read the porch sign as 'A. T. GANTT AND BRO. / GROCERIES - DRY GOODS' and tied it to the firm advertising from January 1908 and to the Gantt mercantile at Fifth & Egan (Mrs. Brice Gantt obituary, 1936).
Date widened from 1918-1924 to c. 1915-1925 and given an evidence basis (car types, Gantt store chronology).
Title made descriptive; rights set from the BLD Calisphere rights statement.

research.original_title: Bogart House From Beaumont Library District
research.description: A large two-story clapboard house stands in heavy snow behind bare deciduous trees, with a small porch at its right-hand entrance, a ladder against the near corner, and outbuildings visible at left — identified in the collection as the Bogart House. Guy Bogart (1883-1957) came to California in 1913 and during the 1920s built his Beaumont home and the Cherry Tree Apartments; he served as Beaumont's mayor and councilman, organized the Cherry Blossom Festival at what became Bogart Park in Cherry Valley, and made his home a gathering place for playwrights, socialists and authors including Upton Sinclair. He died in 1957 and is buried at Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery in Beaumont. Which Bogart residence is shown (the 1920s-built Beaumont home or another family property) is not confirmed, and the snowstorm is undated; heavy lowland snows recorded for inland Southern California include 11 Jan 1930, 15 Jan 1932 (called the heaviest on record in the LA Basin) and 9-11 Jan 1949.
corrections: Attribution confidence downgraded from 'high' to 'probable' — 'from Beaumont Library District' is filename-derived provenance, not an institutional confirmation.

Added evidence-based Guy Bogart context: b. 23 Oct 1883, d. 13 Nov 1957; came to California 1913; built his Beaumont home and the Cherry Tree Apartments in the 1920s; mayor; Cherry Blossom Festival organizer.

research.description: Signed passport-style portrait of Clarendon B. Eyer, the capitalist who as president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company led the syndicate that bought the Beaumont townsite and adjoining lands from a San Francisco bank on August 2, 1907 and relaunched the town. The company's directors and sole stockholders were Eyer and his brothers-in-law Kenneth R. Smoot (vice president) and John D. Reavis — a family enterprise built on the fortune of Eyer's father Daniel Eyer, 'a wealthy mining man of Salt Lake City' (Los Angeles Herald obituary of Eyer's mother, Dec. 7, 1908); Eyer himself was dealing in Salt Lake City real estate in 1906 and told a December 1907 banquet he had come to California from Chicago. From offices at 616 South Broadway, Los Angeles, he ran the land sales, water development, and a forty-newspaper advertising campaign of Beaumont's 1907-1915 apple-boom era, and in April 1908 began a residence for himself at Sixth Street and Magnolia Avenue in Beaumont. The print bears Eyer's signature across the top and an embossed seal at right — the format of a U.S. passport application photograph (photos required from December 1914) — and he appears markedly older here than in his published April 11, 1909 Los Angeles Herald portrait, suggesting c. 1915-1925. His birth and death dates remain unverified.
corrections: Identified the sitter: previously only a filename name, now documented as president and co-owner (with brothers-in-law K. R. Smoot and J. D. Reavis) of the Beaumont Land and Water Company, purchaser of the Beaumont townsite on Aug. 2, 1907.
Re-dated from c. 1890-1915 (low confidence) to c. 1915-1925 based on the passport-photo format (post-Dec. 1914) and his older appearance versus the published 1909 portrait.
Rights changed from Unclear to Permission required (rule 8: unpublished family photo, photographer unknown, created after 1906).
Attribution changed from Unknown to Beaumont Library District (Eyer House and family folder) as scan provenance.

She was an active builder in boom-era Beaumont in her own right: by February 1909 she had taken permits for four cottages in the townsite (Los Angeles Herald, Dec. 13, 1908 and Feb. 28, 1909), and in May 1910 she and daughter Marguerite sailed for Asia aboard the S.S. Eyer portrait in this folder, giving an estimated date of c. 1915-1925. Her 'K.' may be a maiden-name initial — the Eyers' son was named Knowlton K. Eyer — but her maiden name and vital dates remain unverified.

research.description: Oval-matted black-and-white studio portrait of Iola May Stower (b. September 3, 1898, California; d. June 30, 1982, Riverside County), shown head-and-shoulders in a dark dress with white collar, her curled hair swept up and back, glancing down over her shoulder. The photograph survives in its original photographer's mat, but no studio imprint is visible in the scanned area.

research.description: Scan of a printed book page: a halftone portrait plate captioned "MRS. KENNETH R. SMOOT" showing Jane Eyer Smoot (Dec. 17, 1859 - Nov. 25, 1935) white-haired, in a wide-collared dress of the mid-1910s-early 1920s, with the book's binding edge visible at right. Born in Dwight, Illinois, to Daniel Eyer, a Salt Lake City mining man, and Nancy Bennett Eyer, she graduated from the University of Michigan in 1881, married attorney Kenneth R. Smoot in 1883, and in 1894 became president of Highland Park, Illinois' first known woman's club (the Monday Club, renamed the Ossoli Club that October), advocating for woman suffrage in the 1890s. In Beaumont — where her brother Clarendon B. Eyer was president and her husband vice president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company, and where Kenneth later headed the Bank of Beaumont — she remained a civic force: the Beaumont Daily Gazette of May 26, 1932 ran "Tribute Paid to Mrs. K. R. Smoot for Leadership," crediting her and Miss Boulton with the petition crusade that brought gas service to the San Gorgonio Pass. The volume this plate comes from has not been identified; her apparent age and the plate's typography suggest publication c. 1915-1930. She died in Beaumont and is buried at Hillside Memorial Park, Redlands.

research.description: A sepia studio bust portrait of a young man with side-parted hair and a mustache, in a suit with white shirt, striped tie, tie bar, and a small floral spray at the breast pocket — a rephotographed family print. He is Luis Moncada Estrada (1894–1980), who worked as a Southern Pacific track laborer from 1913 to 1947 on the Colton–Indio run through the San Gorgonio Pass, rose to section foreman, and with his wife Emeteria Lira raised ten children, moving the family to Beaumont in 1931, where they lived in an SP section house. He was honored posthumously: Beaumont named Luis Estrada Road for him (the BLD folder's '20 years' 2021 photo implies a 2001 naming), and in 2005 the California State Railroad Museum created a life-size figure of him driving a spike for exhibition. His attire and apparent age of roughly 25–35 fit the existing c. 1915–1930 range, which is retained.

research.original_title: Francis Dowling Sr With Golden State Orchard Truck
research.description: A man identified by the family as Francis Marion Dowling Sr. (1892-1979), in work shirt, trousers, and a brimmed hat, stands beside an early Ford Model T cut down into a flatbed farm truck, gesturing toward its open cab; a placard wired to the stake bed reads 'GOLDEN STATE CHERRY ORCHARD' with a third, illegible smaller line beneath. Behind the truck is a flat-roofed adobe- or plaster-walled building, and orchard branches overhang the frame at left. The wooden-spoke wheels, brass-era body remnants, and runabout-to-truck conversion are typical of working Model Ts in the late 1910s and 1920s, consistent with the catalog's c. 1918-1925 range, when Dowling Sr. was in his late twenties to early thirties. The San Gorgonio Pass was a noted cherry district — Cherry Valley's commercial orchards date from the early 1900s and Beaumont's Cherry Festival began in the 1910s — but no business called 'Golden State Cherry Orchard' could be located in accessible sources, and the family's documented Beaumont orchard on Highway 60 was planted a generation later (early 1950s), so this photograph records an earlier chapter of the family's fruit-growing life whose location is unconfirmed. Note that the sign reads 'Cherry Orchard,' not 'Orchard' as in the old catalog title.
corrections: Title/caption corrected: the placard reads 'Golden State CHERRY Orchard' — the word 'Cherry' was dropped in the original filename-derived title.
Added subject vitals (Francis Sr. 1892-1979) and context distinguishing this 1910s-20s cherry operation from the family's later (early 1950s) Dowling Fruit Orchard on Highway 60.
Attribution upgraded from Unknown to Dowling family collection via Beaumont Library District.
Existing c. 1918-1925 date retained — consistent with the truck type and the subject's apparent age; no evidence found to narrow it.

evidence.label: Geneanet Dowling family tree (fetched HTML): Francis Marion Dowling b. 1892, d. 1979 — in his late 20s to early 30s during the c. 1918-1925 window
Francis Jr. obituary: the family's documented Beaumont orchard (25,000 trees, Highway 60) began after his 1950 UCLA graduation — so the truck photo predates that ranch
Record-Gazette closure story: Dowling Fruit Orchard store opened 1952, closed 2021 — confirming the Highway 60 operation is mid-century, not the orchard in this photo

research.original_title: Kenneth Russell Smoot And Jane Eyer Smoot
research.description: Joint photograph of Kenneth Russell Smoot (Apr. 18, 1857 - May 29, 1932) and Jane Eyer Smoot (1859-1935) with Kenneth's cursive signature above, pixel-identical to the 295x295 px Find a Grave image captioned "Kenneth R Smoot and wife Jane Eyer Smoot Passport photo." It comes from Kenneth's U.S. passport application — his passport was issued November 29, 1920, residence Beaumont, California — in the era when a wife traveling with her husband was commonly included on his passport, so couples were photographed together on one application. Kenneth, born in Washington, D.C. to Dr. Samuel Clement Smoot, attended the University of Michigan, practiced law, and compiled the 'Revised Ordinances of the City of Highland Park' (Illinois) before moving west: by April 1909 he was vice president of the Beaumont Land and Water Company — whose sole stockholders were himself, his brother-in-law Clarendon B. Eyer (president), and John D. Reavis — the family firm behind Beaumont's land boom, with subsidiary San Gorgonio Water Company. He served as president of the Bank of Beaumont until resigning for ill health on March 18, 1932, succeeded by R. P. Stewart, and his Beaumont Daily Gazette obituary called him "one of the city's builders"; he died that May 29 at his home "Quenjuana" on la Mesa Miravilla and is buried at Hillside Memorial Park, Redlands. The couple's son Clement Eyer Smoot (1884-1963), later founder of the Smoot-Holman Company, won team golf gold at the 1904 Olympics.

research.description: A crosshatched artist's sketch of the bearded frontiersman in his wide-brimmed hat — not a photograph, and not a portrait from life. No verified photograph or documented life portrait of Weaver exists, so this is an imagined commemorative likeness, most plausibly drawn in the 1920s. Powell 'Pauline' Weaver, Tennessee-born trapper, scout and prospector of part-Cherokee descent, petitioned Mexican authorities in 1845 (with partner Isaac Williams) for possession of the abandoned Rancho San Gorgonio, lived in an adobe near the future Beaumont running cattle in the pass, and conveyed the ranch to Dr. Isaac W. Smith before leaving in 1857; he later sparked the 1862 La Paz gold rush, camped at the future site of Prescott, and died at Camp Verde, Arizona Territory, on June 21, 1867. He is buried on the Sharlot Hall Museum grounds in Prescott.
corrections: The old caption 'c. 1850s-1860s' implied a photograph from life — no verified photograph of Weaver is known to exist; the defensible claim is 'posthumous likeness', likely 1920s.
Weaver applied for possession of Rancho San Gorgonio in 1845 (with Isaac Williams); no confirmed Mexican land grant to him is documented — avoid 'granted'.

research.original_title: Second Bank Of Beaumont From Beaumont Library District
research.description: Warm-toned street-level view of the arched entrance bay of the second Bank of Beaumont, with a carved archivolt and pediment ornament over the recessed double door, a tall multi-pane window at right, and a parapet cartouche above; a large eucalyptus leans over the sidewalk at left, where two children in coats walk away past distant storefronts. The building was erected in 1923 by Fred Hirsch, a large Beaumont real-estate holder, replacing the town's outgrown first bank; its surviving parapet is incised 'BANK OF BEAUMONT — FOUNDED 1909, ERECTED 1923,' and the building still stands at Fifth Street and California Avenue. The 1923 construction gives the firm start of the date range; the empty street, the children's dress, and the bank's continued operation (its sign came down only in 1950, 'ending a chapter' per the Daily Gazette) are consistent with the collection's c. 1923-1940 estimate. Calisphere's Banning Library District slide of the same building is dated 'circa 1920,' which is impossible for a 1923 building, and its BLD/Calisphere descriptions inconsistently place it at 'Fifth and Egan' — the facade inscription and the surviving building support Fifth and California.
corrections: Confirmed the 1923 floor of the existing 1923-1940 date range from the Calisphere record ('erected in 1923' by Fred Hirsch) and the building's own facade inscription; no change to the range itself.

Located the building at Fifth Street and California Avenue (northeast corner) per the collection folder, the Calisphere item title, and the surviving inscribed building — noting that two Calisphere descriptions contradictorily say 'Fifth and Egan'.
Added context that the Bank of Beaumont sign was removed in 1950 (Daily Gazette, 29 June 1950), bounding the bank's occupancy of the building.

The view runs along Fifth Street: at right stands the classical arched-portal Bank of Beaumont building — the same structure shown in a Banning Library District print labeled "Bank of Beaumont Fifth St. and Egan Ave." — while the left sidewalk shows a jeweler's bracket clock, a barber pole, a drugstore sign, a projecting CAFE sign, and an American flag, with strings of pennants and flags (one bearing a sun disc) crossing the street for some celebration. A later hand added "Main Street, Beaumont, California. Circa 1925" in the lower margin; Frasher's own caption says only "Street Scene". The parked closed sedans read as late-1920s models, so the view may date a few years after the margin note. The catalog scan (956 px) is byte-identical to the BLD copy whose filename records its provenance: shared by Flickr user "clamshack" via Facebook on July 16, 2020.

research.original_title: George Sumner S And S Store On Fifth Street Interior
research.description: Interior of a well-stocked 1920s-era grocery, identified by the collection title as George Sumner's S. and S. store: a produce island stands mid-floor, canned goods line the right wall, and four people pose — two men in shirtsleeves and vests at center, and a mustached man with a bobbed-haired woman behind the counter at right. Wall advertising includes a Kellogg's Krumbles sign ("Build the body with nature's food"), a Kellogg's Bran poster, Alpine Milk tin signs, a Pearl Oil (kerosene) can, a coffee poster ("It's the best I ever tasted"), and National Biscuit Company cartons bearing the "Uneeda Bakers" slogan the company adopted in 1923. The Daily Gazette documents the S. and S. Grocery at the "Corner Egan and Fifth Sts." in weekly ads through 1928, run by George R. Sumner ("Mr. Sumner of the S. & S. Grocery," 22 Mar 1928) with his son-in-law as partner; by January 1931 it advertised as Orange Empire Store No. 25, and by February 1935 the W. M. McDaris family ran it. A November 1928 note about "the grocery now known as the S. & S. grocery" indicates the name — plausibly Sumner & son-in-law — was then fairly new. The store is not among the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere items (searched 2026-07-21).

research.description: A stuccoed, stepped-parapet commercial building at a street corner, identified by the collection title as George Sumner's S. and S. store — the S. and S. "GROCERIES" is painted on a storefront window, a large rooftop sign reads "BEAUMONT," and a vertical two-word sign at the building's right end advertises an unidentified "—— CAFE." Behind it at left stands a two-story building whose roofline sign appears to read "...GENERAL MERCHANDISE" — consistent with the old Gantt mercantile quarter at Fifth & Egan, early Beaumont's main business corner near the depot, though the sign is not legible enough to confirm. Mid-1920s touring cars are parked at the curb with a later truck at right. The store does not appear in the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere collection (searched 2026-07-21).

research.description: A professional 8x10 print corner-mounted on a black album page, the handwritten margin note reading '…at Stewart Ranch' (remainder clipped). research.original_title: Barrio Church Sacred Heart Parish Fr Grace Granados
research.description: A small whitewashed chapel with a squat arched bell gable topped by a cross stands beside a dirt street in Beaumont's Mexican-American barrio, a plain hip-roofed house behind it and a bare winter tree overhead. This is consistent with the original barrio chapel at Olive and B Street, south of Highway 60 and west of Beaumont Avenue, which opened in 1930 as Our Lady of Guadalupe Chapel to serve the Hispanic community of Beaumont and Banning, many of whom worked on the nearby railroad (Diocese of San Bernardino archivist Peter Bradley). For over 25 years it operated as a mission of San Gorgonio Parish in Beaumont and Precious Blood Parish in Banning, until a second church was built on the site in 1956 and the mission was erected as Sacred Heart Parish. The 'Fr' in the working title is donor shorthand for 'from' — the print came from Grace Granados in June 2025 — not a priest's name. The primitive setting and print quality suggest the chapel-era decades before the 1956 replacement.

research.original_title: Steve Lech Postcard Of Fifth Street
research.description: Real photo postcard captioned "Fifth Street (Main) Beaumont, Calif." in the negative, looking along Beaumont's principal business street. At left are a painted wall advertisement for The Gazette ("The home paper for [number obscured] years / advertising [and] commercial printing"), the sign of Harvey's Cafe, and parked sedans of c. 1929-1931 vintage; at right are another cafe, a barber shop, and the Beaumont Garage ("Welding and Machine Work") with a vertical Gilmore Gasoline sign. Harvey's Cafe, run by Harvey O'Day on West Fifth Street between Egan and Wellwood avenues and later Beaumont's bus depot, first appears in the Daily Gazette on 6 October 1932 and is absent from the digitized 1928-1931 issues, so the view is c. 1932 at the earliest; the cafe's old building was remodeled for other use in 1944. The Beaumont Garage was a much older institution, advertising "Now Open for Business" (W. D. Lewis, manager) in October 1908, trading as Beaumont Garage & Machine Works by 1916, and purchased by M. Torres (née Velasquez, 1917-2005), flowers pinned in her curled 1940s-style hair; the partial red side-panel text ('For three… passed…') is the menu's family-history blurb. Ramona was born Jan. 24, 1917 in Douglas, Arizona, married Frank Mora Torres in Los Angeles on Feb. 24, 1935, and in 1972 the couple opened Ramona's Restaurant at 249 W. Sixth St., Beaumont. Press coverage of the restaurant's Jan. 11, 2025 closing noted that her black-and-white portrait 'hangs on a wall in the dining room and decorates the menu' — this image is that menu reproduction. The restaurant ran 52 years under three generations: the founders, then daughter Christine and Gil Vargas Sr. from about 1982, then grandchildren Gil Jr., Adrian and Maritza Vargas until closing. The underlying portrait likely dates from about the 1940s, when Ramona was in her twenties; the physical menu photographed here is modern, from the restaurant's final years.

Per BLD's Calisphere record the building housed City Hall and the police station, with city offices remaining until the mid-1980s; the fire department stayed until its Maple Avenue station was completed c. 1969. A partially legible sign on the commercial building at far right appears to read '…HARDWARE & LUMBER,' consistent with the Beaumont Hardware and Lumber store documented at Fifth and Grace Streets. The scan was received from Karen Sumner Noordman on January 12, 2023, per the filename.

research.original_title: Beaumont Railroad Women Swept The Tracks
research.description: Thirteen women in work shirts, trousers and broad-brimmed hats pose on the railroad right-of-way at Beaumont, at least one holding a track maul; a period ink inscription across the top of the print reads 'Female R.R. Crew', with a first name written above or beside each woman. Legible names in the standing row read Margarita (or Marguerite), Estella, Felicitas, Esther, Emilia, Lupe, Viola(?), and Soledad; the kneeling row includes Lily, Tresie(?), Mary, and Minnie (right margin). The predominantly Spanish given names are consistent with the Mexican-American railroad families of Beaumont's barrio who staffed Southern Pacific's Sunset Route section gangs (compare the catalog's Estrada section-house photographs). Women's track maintenance crews were essentially a WWII labor-shortage phenomenon — roughly 116,000 women worked U.S. railroads by war's end, and Southern Pacific documented hiring Mexican-American women as track workers ('traqueras') — so the photo almost certainly dates c. 1942-1945, not the 1915-1940 range previously carried. The photographer and the family that contributed the print are unrecorded.
corrections: Retitled from 'Beaumont Railroad Women Swept The Tracks' to follow the photograph's own inscription, 'Female R.R. Crew'.
Date moved from c. 1915-1940 to c. 1942-1945: women's track section crews were a WWII labor-shortage phenomenon, and the clothing fits the 1940s.
Transcribed the individual first names inscribed above each woman (Margarita, Estella, Felicitas, Esther, Emilia, Lupe, Viola?, Soledad; Lily, Tresie?, Mary, Minnie).

The deodars that line both sides of Beaumont Avenue from present Oak Valley Parkway north through Cherry Valley toward Oak Glen were planted in the 1930s and grew into the Pass Area's celebrated "evergreen tunnel," a local landmark residents have repeatedly organized to protect (Record-Gazette). In this frame the trees already stand several times the height of the car — well-established plantings of roughly 15-25 years — which, with the late-1940s body style of the automobile, places the photograph around 1950. The scan was saved from an eBay listing; the card's photographer/publisher and back are unrecorded.

research.description: Square-format snapshot of a family meal in a small board-walled room the donor identifies as the Estradas' railroad section house: adults and children crowd a table set with bottles and glasses beneath an open shelf of dishes, with floral wallpaper and exposed ceiling boards typical of standard railroad section dwellings. A girl with braided hair and a large white hair bow kneels on a bench in the foreground, a teenage boy faces the camera at center, and an older balding man — plausibly Luis Estrada — sits at the rear right. The 1950 census places Luis and Emeteria Estrada's Beaumont household with six children born c. 1930–1947, several of whom match the ages of the children here, and the snapshot format and furnishings suggest the late 1940s to early 1950s. The specific occasion is unrecorded. The section house's location is not yet confirmed; the census gives the family's April 1950 dwelling as house number 211 on a street whose name is illegible on the sheet.

research.original_title: 6Th St Fr Bmt High Yearbook Donated By Leslie Rios
research.description: A photographed page from the 1946 Beaumont High School annual: a halftone street view printed above the start of the yearbook's index (the heading 'Index' and the first senior entries, beginning 'Smith, Pat,' are visible below the image). The photograph looks across a wide intersection on Sixth Street, Beaumont's main commercial street, which carried U.S. Highway 99 through town before the freeway era — Wikipedia's San Gorgonio Pass article documents 6th Street in Beaumont as an old section of U.S. 99. On the left corner is a Standard Stations, Inc. service station beneath a Chevron 'Supreme Gasoline' billboard; beyond it a storefront signed '—ING CENTER' carries a Coca-Cola sign, and at the right edge a Mobilgas shield with the Flying Red Horse marks a competing station — a gasoline strip typical of a US 99 highway town. Every legible automobile is a prewar model, consistent with an exposure around 1945–46, when the annual went to press before postwar cars were common on the street. The catalog copy is a handheld phone photo (4032×3024) of the printed page from the yearbook Leslie A. Rios III donated in November 2020, not a scan of an original print.

research.description: Real photo postcard by Frasher Fotos of Pomona (the Frasher's logo and negative number F6331 are printed in the margin), captioned 'Beaumont, Calif. on U.S. Highways 60 and 99.' The theatre marquee advertises Dorothy Lamour in 'Masquerade in Mexico' — a Paramount picture released December 3, 1945 — on a double bill with the 1940 Warner Bros. title 'City for Conquest,' which dates the exposure to c. 1946. Sixth Street carried the combined US 60/99 highway traffic through Beaumont, which is why Frasher's roadside series covered this strip. Scanned from a card in the Leslie A. Rios III postcard collection.

research.description: Roughly sixty uniformed musicians of the Beaumont Union High School band pose in rows on the steps of a two-story school building beneath a hanging banner lettered 'BEAUMONT UNION HIGH SCHOOL BAND' (legible under magnification of the master file), with sousaphones at the rear corners, majorette-uniformed girls kneeling at the flanks, and a drum majorette and a small mascot girl seated front and center among the bass drums. 'Beaumont Union High School' was the school's formal name in this era — a Record-Gazette obituary records a 1943 graduate under that name. The page comes from the 1949 annual, so the photograph dates to the 1948–49 school year. The building behind the band is presumably on the historic BHS campus — Beaumont's first high school building went up in 1911, and the Record-Gazette described BHS's '107-year-old campus' still hosting football in 2018 — but the source folder's claim that the old high school is 'now City Hall' has not been independently verified; the Beaumont Civic Center campus is documented to incorporate former school-district property (the old Summit School parcel behind the Civic Center, bought by the city in 2009). The catalog copy is a phone photo of the printed yearbook page from the volume donated by Leslie A. Rios III in November 2020.

research.description: Halftone reproduction (screened, rephotographed from a printed page) of four men gathered around bushel baskets of apples on a table, three of them holding up filled mesh bags. The elderly, bald man in round glasses second from right is Guy Bogart (23 Oct 1883 - 13 Nov 1957), matching his appearance in the 1955 BLD/Calisphere portrait at his 545 Euclid Ave desk. Bogart, a former Los Angeles Times reporter and cousin of Humphrey Bogart, moved to Beaumont in 1923, was elected to the city council in 1924, and served as mayor and as president of the Beaumont Chamber of Commerce; Bogart Park and its festival carry his name. The companions' 1950s sport shirts and eyewear and Bogart's advanced age date the scene to roughly 1950-1957, bounded by his death in November 1957. The occasion and the other three men are unidentified.

research.original_title: Laura May Stewart In The Room On Their Ranch Where She Collected Family Items
research.description: An elderly Laura May Stewart, in glasses and a checked dress, holds a rifle above a stock saddle; a coiled riata hangs on the wall at right and framed photographs of ranch and range scenes hang behind her — the room at the Stewart ranch where she gathered her family's pioneer relics. Stewart (c. 1885-1974) was one of five children of Reznor Perry Stewart and Mary Elizabeth Stewart, Pass pioneers whose 1883 homestead grew to more than 2,200 acres of Beaumont-Banning ranch land (today's Sun Lakes and Four Seasons areas), partly purchased from the Southern Pacific Railroad. Before her death in 1974 at age 89 she endowed the $1.2 million Laura May Stewart Trust, whose successor foundation still makes grants to Banning and Beaumont charities; the Trust is also the rights holder named on Stewart photographs in the Beaumont Library District's Calisphere collection. A halftone dot screen is clearly visible across this copy, showing it was re-photographed from a printed publication — most likely a local newspaper or history feature — which has not yet been identified.

research.original_title: Beaumont Map Diagonal Streets To Left Were Mapped By George C Egan
research.description: Printed street map titled 'City of Beaumont, California,' credited in the plate 'Map furnished courtesy Don Stock—Realtor,' with hand-drawn annotations marking U.S. Highways 70/99 and 60, the 'State Highway' to Banning along Sixth Street, the S.P. Railway, an 'Airport' northwest of town, and the '3 Ring Ranch.' Don Stock appears in the Beaumont Gazette from 1949 and as principal of the Grant and Stock realty firm on Fifth Street from early 1950, and the Three Ring Ranch — George and Connie Ring's thoroughbred farm on Beaumont's western outskirts — first appears in the papers in September 1951, so the map dates to roughly the 1950s, before the 1964 renumbering that replaced US 70/99 with Interstate 10. The working title repeats a local tradition that the diagonal streets at lower left were mapped by George C. Egan: Egan built the first store in the townsite (then called San Gorgonio) in June 1884 on California Avenue, came to own nearly the whole townsite, and sold out in fall 1886 to the Southern California Investment Company, which renamed the town Beaumont in 1887. The diagonal grid runs parallel to the Southern Pacific tracks and includes Egan Avenue (named for the pioneer) and Grace Avenue (named for his daughter), so it does preserve the original 1880s San Gorgonio townsite orientation — though Holmes' 1912 county history credits the investment company, not Egan personally, with laying out some twenty miles of streets.
corrections: Re-dated from 1887-1895 to c. 1950s: the artifact is a mid-20th-century printed map (US 70/99 and 60 highway shields, realtor Don Stock credit, Three Ring Ranch and airport annotations), not the 1887 plat the old caption implied.

Reframed the Egan claim: Egan's connection is that the diagonal street grid (including Egan and Grace avenues, named for him and his daughter per Holmes 1912) preserves the 1880s San Gorgonio townsite orientation; Holmes credits the Southern California Investment Company with the ~20 miles of streets laid out in 1887, so 'mapped by George C. Egan' is kept only as local tradition.
Attribution upgraded from 'Unknown' to the map's own printed credit (Don Stock, Realtor).

That anchors this photograph at 1955, two years before Bogart's death; he is buried in Stewart Sunnyslope Cemetery, Beaumont.

research.original_title: Sacred Heart Barrio Church From Leslie Rios
research.description: A color slide-era view of families in Sunday best leaving Sacred Heart Church in Beaumont's barrio: girls in white First Communion-style dresses with veils and floral headpieces, a girl in a blue coat, boys in white shirts, and women in 1950s coats and headscarves on wet pavement. The church is the second building, constructed in 1956 at Olive and B Street when the Our Lady of Guadalupe mission was erected as Sacred Heart Parish — textured white stucco, red mission-tile trim, round stained-glass window over the canopied door, and a corner tower with a Virgin statue in its niche. A light-blue mid-1950s Chevrolet at left carries a 1956-issue yellow California plate (CWE 630), the base used through 1962 before the 1963 gold-on-black plates, and a dark early-1950s Chrysler-family sedan sits at right, bracketing the photo between the 1956 construction and 1962. The parish, whose members largely worked on the railroad, was closed by the Diocese of San Diego on March 5, 1964, making this one of the few color records of its short life as a full parish.

research.original_title: Sared Heart Parish In Beaumont Barrio Date
research.description: A printed halftone reproduction (visible CMYK registration fringing indicates a scan from a publication, not an original print) showing the second Sacred Heart church: a gable-fronted stucco building with a round window over the entrance, a corner bell tower with open belfry, pyramidal tile cap and cross, and a small tile-roofed outbuilding at right. The massing, round window, corner tower, and outbuilding match the church in the Leslie A. Rios III color slide of this parish, identifying it as the second church built in 1956 at Olive and B Street, when the 25-year-old Our Lady of Guadalupe mission was erected as Sacred Heart Parish. Rev. Felix Callymore was its first pastor (1956-1962), followed by Rev. Andre Begeron (1962, 1963-1964); the parish was poor — Sunday collections totaled about $8 — and after San Gorgonio Parish completed its own new church in 1958, membership drained away. The Diocese of San Diego closed Sacred Heart Parish on March 5, 1964, and the building was sold to a local Catholic family for $4,000. The photograph therefore most likely dates from the parish's 1956-1964 lifetime, reproduced later in an unidentified newspaper or newsletter.

research.original_title: First Christian Church Egan Ave Probably Late 1950S A
research.description: Congregants file down the broad corner steps of the First Christian Church at 701 Egan Avenue (northwest corner of 7th and Egan), a castellated corner-tower church built of rusticated 'ornate' concrete block with twin round-arched louvered tower openings, oculus gable vents, and arched stained-glass windows. Women in hats and long coats descend the steps; a 1940s GM fastback sedan (California plate BHN 623) waits at the curb. The signboard beside the door reads 'First Christian Church / Minister F. E. Wodell / Bible School 9:30 AM / Worship 11:00 AM / Youth Groups 5:30 PM.' Rev. Frank E. Wodell is documented as pastor of the Beaumont (First) Christian Church from at least mid-1957 and was given a farewell in early March 1961, with successor Chester A. Rice installed that same month — dating the photograph to c. 1957-1961 and confirming the folder's 'probably late 1950s' guess. The BLD/Calisphere record for a related view states the building was built by John J. McCoy in 1885 as an Episcopal church, though its concrete-block construction is more typical of c. 1905-1915.

research.description: Black-and-white snapshot of Ramona V. Torres (1917-2005) and Frank Mora Torres (1913-2005) standing arm-in-arm at the end of a café lunch counter — Ramona in a floral shirtwaist dress, Frank in a white shirt — with back-counter equipment, an acoustic-tile ceiling, and what appears to be a framed picture of a woman displayed on the back counter behind them. The couple opened Ramona's Restaurant at 249 W. Sixth St., Beaumont in 1972, and press coverage records that a black-and-white portrait of Ramona hung in its dining room, so this may be the interior of Ramona's itself or an earlier café where the couple worked; the location is unconfirmed. Frank, born 1913 in Michoacán, was a WWII Army sergeant; Ramona, born 1917 in Douglas, Arizona, was the restaurant's namesake, and their descendants ran it until Jan. 11, 2025. The couple's apparent middle age and Ramona's full-skirted dress are consistent with the existing c. 1960s dating, though a date in the restaurant's first years (early-to-mid 1970s) cannot be excluded.

research.description: Color studio portrait of an elderly couple: Francis Marion Dowling Sr. (b. April 9, 1892, Bethany, Brooke County, West Virginia; d. February 17, 1979, Riverside County, CA) in a light suit and browline glasses, and his wife Iola May (Stower) Dowling (b. September 3, 1898; d. June 30, 1982) in a lace dress with pearl necklace and earrings. The couple married May 25, 1924 in Glendora, CA, and later settled in Beaumont, where Francis Sr. and his son Francis Jr. planted some 25,000 fruit trees, the start of the Dowling Fruit Orchard on Highway 60 (fruit stand opened 1952, operated until 2021). Both appear to be in their mid-70s to 80s, and the color print, his browline glasses, and her dress style all point to the late 1960s-1970s; the photo must predate his death in February 1979. The print shows heavy red/magenta dye shift typical of aging chromogenic prints of that era. The catalog's former date of c. 1900-1920 was impossible given the sitters' ages and color photography.

research.description: Black-and-white snapshot of Ramona V.
