research.description: Full page 3 of The Daily Record-Gazette (Banning) for Friday, March 21, 1969, combining an architect's two-part rendering of the rock-faced 'City of Beaumont Fire Station' with the halftone 'Clearing Fire Station Land', in which men confer beside a bulldozer on the graded site. The article, legible in the scan, reports that official groundbreaking took place the morning of Nov. 27, 1968 at 650 Maple Ave. just north of Sixth St.; that the 3,600-square-foot central station on a 14,500-square-foot site would let the police department under chief Jack Richardson expand into the old fire station at City Hall; that fire chief Mickey Wright planned a second station south of the freeway and Southern Pacific tracks (L.R. Daniel offering property at B St. and Minnesota Ave.); and that citizen Fred Hirsch contracted to build the $30,000 facility, repaid by the city over a period of years. The completed station — today Fire Station 66, addressed 628 Maple Ave. — appears in 1971 Beaumont Library District photographs on Calisphere; the 650 vs. 628 Maple address difference between the article and today's station is noted but unresolved.

research.description: Snapshot of a framed presentation watercolor showing a long, low, nearly windowless masonry school with vertical wood-tone accent panels, lawns, young trees, a flagpole and figures, with pass foothills behind; the credit plate reads 'Harry T. MacDonald & Associates, Architecture-Planning' and the partially cropped title block reads '[...]REET SCHOOL / [...]IED SCHOOL DISTRICT.' MacDonald was the architect of record for Beaumont's Summit School: he was introduced at its dedication on May 19, 1974, and the Beaumont Unified School District board accepted the completed school in late February 1974, so this rendering belongs to the design/construction phase, c. 1970-74. Summit School replaced the adjacent Sixth Street School — the 1928 high school building that failed Field Act earthquake standards and was sold to the city to become the Beaumont Civic Center — which is very likely the '...Street School' working title on the cropped label, applied before the board adopted the historic Summit name. That name reaches back to the pioneer Summit School District, organized when the Beaumont area was still in San Bernardino County; the district's 1890 school bell was inscribed 'Bought for Summit School District, San Bernardino County, Cal.' The campus, behind the Civic Center between Orange and Palm avenues, was built on nearly the exact site of the earlier Magnolia School, later housed Mountain View Middle School, and was ultimately sold to the city of Beaumont for its civic-center campus.
corrections: Identified the rendering as the project drawing for the Summit School completed in 1974 — not a generic 'c. 1960s-1970s' school rendering; date narrowed from 1962-1975 to c. 1970-1974.

Read the credit plate off the full-resolution source: 'Harry T. MacDonald & Associates, Architecture-Planning', and confirmed via the Sun-Telegram that MacDonald was Summit School's architect (introduced at the May 19, 1974 dedication).

Documented that the cropped title block reads '[...]REET SCHOOL / [...]IED SCHOOL DISTRICT' — the artwork is NOT labeled 'Summit School'; it very likely carries the working title of the Sixth Street School replacement project, the only documented '... Street School' in Beaumont USD.

Added the name's lineage: Summit School District was Beaumont's pioneer school district (1890 bell inscribed 'Summit School District, San Bernardino County'; district election notices in the 1909 Daily Gazette), and the campus's later life as Mountain View Middle School before sale to the city.

research.description: Color class portrait of roughly 33 kindergartners posed in four rows on a lawn beneath autumn-colored trees, their young teacher standing at right, with a black letter-board reading 'WELLWOOD SCHOOL / MISS PRITCHETT / KINDERGARTEN / 1971-72.' The teacher is very probably Penny Pritchett, recorded in the San Bernardino Sun of September 1, 1974 as a teacher at Wellwood School in Beaumont. Wellwood School stood near Seventh Street and Elm Avenue and was one of Beaumont's two long-running elementary campuses alongside Palm School; it descended from the 1890 'Olive school' of the pioneer Summit School District, whose bell was inscribed 'Bought for Summit School District, San Bernardino County, Cal.' By this era it was a Beaumont Unified School District school — Anne Pickett, later BUSD superintendent, taught at Wellwood and served as principal of Wellwood and Palm in the 1970s-80s. The fall foliage indicates the standard autumn sitting, so the photograph was probably taken in October-November 1971 by an as-yet-unidentified school portrait studio.

research.description: Eight men of the Beaumont Fire Department line up before the open apparatus bay of their station in 1972 — seven in khaki uniform shirts with shoulder patches (the second man from left wears a tie, possibly the chief), one at right in civilian sweater, with an engine's beacon and speaker visible in the bay behind them. The building's diamond-pattern concrete block and decorative screen-block match the fire station built on Maple Avenue in 1969 (its construction was covered in the Record-Gazette of March 21, 1969 — clippings in this same source folder) and the station shown in the Beaumont Library District's 1971 photographs on Calisphere; the building serves today as Riverside County Fire Station 66, 628 Maple Avenue. In 1972 Beaumont still ran its own combination paid-and-volunteer department; six years later, on November 28, 1978, the Record-Gazette reported the City Council's vote to contract fire services to the California Department of Forestry, and the city has been served by CDF/Riverside County Fire since 1978. The chief at the time was likely Mickey Wright, named to the post in October 1967 after Clarence 'Pappy' Lewis retired, per a Record-Gazette clipping of April 30, 1968 in this collection. The file is a February 10, 2009 flatbed scan of a black-and-white print.

research.description: A black-and-white print of the Beaumont Fire Department's antique hand-drawn hose cart, loaded with rolled hose and carrying a painted 'BEAUMONT FIRE DEPT' sign, displayed on the lawn of the city fire station at 628 Maple Avenue — the street number '628' visible over the garage matches the address on the department's 1977 letterhead elsewhere in this collection, and the building still serves as Riverside County Fire Station 66. research.description: A firefighter in black helmet and red suspenders sits at the wheel of the Beaumont Fire Department's white open-cab antique pumper, gold-lettered 'BEAUMONT FIRE DEPARTMENT / ENGINE CO. No. 2,' with a hose reel mounted behind the cab and ground ladders alongside — rolling in Beaumont's annual Cherry Festival parade, annotated late 1970s. The same engine, identified in the department archive as a LaFrance kept for parade duty, appears parked at the Maple Avenue fire station in a 1971 archive photo in this collection ('...LaFrance fire engine used for parades... dated 1971'), so the make rests on that annotation rather than on visible markings. The Cherry Festival began in 1918 and its parade is documented from 1919 (a Calisphere item titled 'The Cherry Festival Parade, 1919' survives in the Beaumont Library District collection); the festival celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2018. A late-1970s date would place this appearance at the very end of the municipal department, which passed to CDF/Riverside County in 1978. The digital file is itself an iPhone re-photograph (June 11, 2023 per EXIF) of a silk-finish color print, whose stock is consistent with the 1970s.

research.description: A typed letter on City of Beaumont Fire Department letterhead — 628 Maple Avenue, Michael C. Diebner, Fire Chief, with a red emblem of a horse-drawn fire wagon — dated May 26, 1977 and addressed to Emma Estrada at 218 'B' Street, Beaumont. It confirms that the department's rescue unit responded to her address that day 'as a public service without charge,' warns that other agencies may bill for similar services, and invites her to call again at need; it is signed by John McLaughlin, Engineer, on the chief's behalf. McLaughlin is corroborated as a Beaumont FD member by a 1976 photo with fireman Scott DeForge in this same collection folder, and Diebner is the chief who eighteen months later presented the CDF contract that ended the city-run department (Record-Gazette, Nov. 28, 1978, also in this catalog). The letter is a small primary document of the city-run department's final years — free rescue service was one of the points argued when the council voted to contract fire services to the state in 1978 — and it reached the collection through the Estrada family, whose materials appear throughout this catalog.

research.original_title: Council Votes To Contract Fire Services With Cdf News Clip From Record Gazette
research.description: Front page of the Record-Gazette (Banning; masthead: 'The Community Voice of the San Gorgonio Pass Since 1908'), 70th year, No. 232, Tuesday, November 28, 1978, carrying Jim Lyntton's report 'Council Votes To Contract Fire Services With CDF.' The Beaumont City Council, rejecting a citizens' 'S.O.S.' (Save Our Services) campaign, voted 4–1 — Councilman J.E. 'Duke' DeForge dissenting — to contract city fire services to the California Division of Forestry beginning December 1, 1978, at an estimated $102,016 a year including $64,068 in salaries. Fire Chief Michael Diebner presented a line-by-line explanation of the contract; city firefighters were approved for transfer to CDF with raises (including fireman Scott DeForge), the fire house was to be leased to the county for $3 a year, and City Manager Glenn Sparks and citizens debated liability coverage and Proposition 13's toll on the city budget. The page marks the end of Beaumont's city-run fire department: the city's own website confirms it has contracted with CDF (now CAL FIRE)/Riverside County Fire ever since. The Record-Gazette's 1968–1993 run is digitized in the California Digital Newspaper Collection at UC Riverside, where this issue should be verifiable.

The props are the classic set pieces of a home-hazard demonstration (kitchen, curtain, and bedding fires) of the kind fire departments staged for schools and Fire Prevention Week audiences. McLaughlin is documented in this collection as a Beaumont Fire Department engineer — he signed the department's May 26, 1977 letter to Emma Estrada and appears in a 1976 photo with fireman Scott DeForge — and after December 1978 Beaumont's fire protection was run under contract by CDF/Riverside County, so an early-1980s demonstration would have been under that arrangement. The catalog had flattened the folder's 'early 1980s' descriptor to an exact 1980; the date is restored here as a 1980–1984 range.

research.original_title: Francis Dowling Jr And Son John Dowling Sorting Cherries
research.description: Color snapshot inside a packing room: an elderly Francis Dowling Jr. in a navy T-shirt and green-billed mesh cap smiles at the camera while his son John, in a white T-shirt and jeans, sorts dark cherries in a wooden bin; an orange 'WATER HEATER' sign is taped to the door at left and a box marked 'FRESH' sits at right, with customers visible in the sales room beyond. Francis Marion Dowling Jr. (Feb 13, 1925 – Oct 8, 2016) founded Dowling Fruit Orchards in 1952, planting some 25,000 trees with his father; the stand at 38021 Highway 60 in Beaumont became a local institution, with cherries among its signature crops. John Dowling (born c. 1962; aged 59 when the orchard closed in November 2021) ran the business with his wife Shelly in its final years. research.original_title: Francis Dowling Jr With Clamp Truck
research.description: A color print showing Dowling Fruit Orchard founder Francis Marion Dowling Jr. (1925-2016) in a red plaid jacket, wheeling stacked cartons labeled 'Cherries' on a tall wooden-framed hand truck (called a 'clamp truck' in the collection filename) through the doorway of his Beaumont stand, with jam shelves, cooler doors, and hand-lettered 'No shirts, no service' and 'No pets allowed in store' signs behind him. Dowling, a Beaumont High valedictorian and WWII Navy electronics technician, earned a horticulture degree at UCLA in 1950, bought land on US Highway 60, planted some 25,000 fruit trees with his father Francis Sr., and opened the roadside store in 1952. Cherry season was his favorite time of year, and he was named honored citizen of Beaumont's 1993 Cherry Festival. His evident age here (late 80s) places the photo in roughly the last decade of his life; the file's 2022 EXIF timestamp is a Windows Photo Editor digitization date, not the capture date.

Earlier catalog wording called this a photo of a 'statue' and, on review, a living man — it is neither: it is a close-up of the museum's exhibit figure of Estrada.

research.description: Interior view at the California State Railroad Museum in Sacramento showing the museum's life-size figure of Luis Estrada in work clothes straining on a lining bar over the rails, with a pickaxe and wheelbarrow beside him and a steam locomotive numbered 4466 on its smokebox behind; a museum visitor stands at left beyond the barrier rails. corrections: Identified the exhibit figure as the California State Railroad Museum's 2005 life-size figure OF Luis Estrada (per CSRM finding aid MS 871); earlier notes hedged the Estrada connection as an unverified family association and referred to a 'statue.'

research.original_title: City Of Beaumont Work And Dress Uniforms
research.description: A modern color photograph (iPhone 7, March 27, 2021 per EXIF) of a museum-style display of City of Beaumont Fire Department uniforms, with an unidentified man — plausibly a retired Beaumont firefighter or the uniforms' donor — posing beside it. The display holds a khaki short-sleeve work uniform with badge and Beaumont shoulder patch, a navy dress uniform with peaked cap, badge, and 'Beaumont Fire' shoulder patch on a mannequin, a yellow wildland jacket at left, and a brass nozzle at the base, all set against an enlarged black-and-white photograph of firefighters at work. The uniforms date from the municipal fire department era, which ended when the City Council voted in November 1978 to contract fire protection to the California Department of Forestry — documented by a Record-Gazette 11-28-78 clipping in the same source folder and by the city's official statement that it has contracted with Riverside County Fire/CAL FIRE 'since 1978.' The exhibit venue is unconfirmed; the interior shows a tiled floor, wood-and-glass double doors, and an antique stove. The khaki shirt and badge in this display also appear in a separate November 2020 close-up photo in this collection (img_0f63f186060123e4), taken with the same iPhone 7.
corrections: Re-dated from c. 1960-1978 to March 27, 2021: the catalog treated this as a vintage photograph, but EXIF proves it is a modern iPhone photo of exhibited pre-1978 artifacts.

research.description: Digital photograph of John Dowling, son of founder Francis Dowling Jr., standing among retired ranch equipment in the old packing barn at Dowling Fruit Orchard, wearing a shirt embroidered with the store's logo. EXIF data shows it was taken with an Apple iPhone 7 on November 19, 2021 at 11:51 a.m. — days before the stand closed for good at the end of that month, and one day before the Record-Gazette published its closure story. John (59 at closing, so born c. 1962) had worked the stand full-time since 1989 and ran it with his wife Shelly in its final years, when the property had diminished from 62 to about 31 acres. This is not one of the Record-Gazette's photos (those were credited to writer David James Heiss and show different scenes); it comes from the same iPhone 7 that shot this collection's storefront-banners photo later the same day, evidently a private documentation visit during the stand's final weeks.
